Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. Above 66 degC the drive derates its speed, adding about 0.8 s to the cycle for every degree above that point, so the cell cycle time rises and stations downstream are starved. The 72 degC alarm comes before the 80 degC trip.

| Trip S-ST20-SRV-OT or S-ST30-SRV-OT at 80 degC | Sustained overheating not corrected at the alarm stage | Check coolant flow (ST30), the cabinet fan and the gun mechanics for binding | Let the drive cool; restart only after the cause is found |

This derating penalty adds 0.8 s to cycle duration for every degree Celsius above 66 degC. As speed falls, cell cycle time rises past the nominal 50 s standard, causing downstream starvation. If temperature reaches 72 degC, the cell issues an over-temperature alarm, followed by a total cell trip at 80 degC.

citations.quote: | A-ST10-CYC-HI | ST10 Press: cycle time high | `cycle_time_s` above 58 s; alarm: the station keeps running |

| ST10 cycle time stepped up at a shift start and stays at the new level; process signals normal | Timer or dwell parameter changed at the changeover (wrong value, wrong recipe, or a trial value left active) | Compare the active parameter set with the last approved copy; check the parameter log for the shift start | Restore the approved value under change control; record the deviation |

Hydraulic wear develops over hours to days, not at a changeover. Four failure modes are common: internal pump leakage, a sluggish (lagging) switching valve, loss of accumulator precharge, and loss of cooler efficiency. Each moves pressure, motor current, oil temperature, vibration and cycle time in its own pattern; use Table 6-3 to tell them apart. All four lengthen the press cycle, which starves the stations downstream.

Regardless of the specific mechanism, hydraulic degradation inevitably lengthens cycle_time_s beyond the nominal 48 s value, eventually exceeding the 58 s alarm threshold and starving downstream stations such as the ST20 weld cell.

citations.quote: | A-ST20-SRVT-HI | ST20 Weld cell A: servo temperature high | `servo_temp_c` above 72 degC; alarm: the station keeps running |

Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. Above 66 degC the drive derates its speed, adding about 0.8 s to the cycle for every degree above that point, so the cell cycle time rises and stations downstream are starved. The 72 degC alarm comes before the 80 degC trip. A failing cabinet fan is often audible before the trip.
On ST30, check coolant flow first: a servo temperature rise that follows a fall in coolant flow is a cooling-circuit problem (see Section 6.4), not a drive problem.

| `servo_temp_c` above 65 degC, cycle time normal | Cabinet fan failing or filter mat clogged; high ambient temperature | Listen to the cabinet fan; inspect the filter mat; compare cabinet and ambient temperature | Clean or replace the filter mat; replace the fan (see Table 7-1) |

citations.quote: | A-ST20-GUN-FRC / A-ST30-GUN-FRC | gun force not reached (weld cells) | Often the first sign of low supply air at the cells; see Section 6.2 |

When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows. The weld cells see their regulated gun air fall shortly after; gun force alarms follow, and when gun air reaches each cell's own low limit (see the weld cell manual) the supply-air interlock stops that cell.

The header pressure drops below the 6.2 bar cut-in setting until it breaches the 5.6 bar low alarm limit, triggering alarm A-UTAIR-HDR-LO. Shortly after header pressure declines, downstream air to the weld guns drops below the 5.6 bar regulator setting. Gun force alarms follow, and once gun pressure falls to the internal low limit of ST20 or ST30, the supply-air interlock halts cell operation.

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. Above 66 degC the drive derates its speed, adding about 0.8 s to the cycle for every degree above that point, so the cell cycle time rises and stations downstream are starved. The 72 degC alarm comes before the 80 degC trip. A failing cabinet fan is often audible before the trip.

- On ST30, check coolant flow first: a servo temperature rise that follows a fall in coolant flow is a cooling-circuit problem (see Section 6.4), not a drive problem.
- A servo temperature rise with normal coolant flow and a cabinet fan that is noisy, slow or stopped points to the cabinet cooling fan or a clogged cabinet filter.
- A servo temperature reading that climbs while cycle time, weld current and coolant flow stay normal may be an instrument problem; see Section 6.8.

citations.quote: | A-ST20-WLD-QA / A-ST30-WLD-QA | weld monitor: weld energy out of band | Weld outside its current/resistance window; see Section 6.2 |

Tip resistance (`tip_resistance_mohm`) climbs steadily over hours from about 0.15 mOhm towards the 0.185 mOhm alarm limit as the tip faces pick up coating material and oxide (which raises contact resistance) and lose their shape, while the current stepper raises weld current (`weld_current_ka`) to compensate. citations.quote: Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. Above 66 degC the drive derates its speed, adding about 0.8 s to the cycle for every degree above that point, so the cell cycle time rises and stations downstream are starved. On ST30, check coolant flow first: a servo temperature rise that follows a fall in coolant flow is a cooling-circuit problem (see Section 6.4), not a drive problem.

When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows. The weld cells see their regulated gun air fall shortly after; gun force alarms follow, and when gun air reaches each cell's own low limit (see the weld cell manual) the supply-air interlock stops that cell. A leak is often audible as a hiss at the leak point.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.
A fall in gun air pressure at ST20 and ST30 at the same time, after the header pressure has fallen, places the cause in the air supply, not in the weld cells.

citations.quote: Regulated gun air (`air_pressure_bar`) normally sits at 5.6 bar within 5.3 to 5.9 bar. Below 5 bar the cell raises a low-air alarm; at 4.6 bar the supply-air interlock stops the cell. Gun force alarms (A-ST20-GUN-FRC, A-ST30-GUN-FRC) can appear as the air falls.

When gun air pressure falls at ST20 and ST30 together, the cause is upstream in the plant air supply; check the header pressure (see Section 6.2 of AM-CA-01 (Plant Air System and Utilities)) before working on either cell.
When gun air falls at one cell only, check that cell's filter-regulator, drop-leg ball valve and quick couplings.

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |
| A-UTAIR-HDR-LO | Plant air compressor and header: header pressure low | `header_pressure_bar` below 5.6 bar; alarm: the station keeps running |

citations.quote: Regulated gun air (`air_pressure_bar`) normally sits at 5.6 bar within 5.3 to 5.9 bar. Below 5 bar the cell raises a low-air alarm; at 4.6 bar the supply-air interlock stops the cell. Gun force alarms (A-ST20-GUN-FRC, A-ST30-GUN-FRC) can appear as the air falls.

When gun air pressure falls at ST20 and ST30 together, the cause is upstream in the plant air supply; check the header pressure (see Section 6.2 of AM-CA-01 (Plant Air System and Utilities)) before working on either cell.
When gun air falls at one cell only, check that cell's filter-regulator, drop-leg ball valve and quick couplings.
| Gun air low at both ST20 and ST30 | Plant air header pressure low (leak or compressor problem) | Check `header_pressure_bar` on UT-AIR | Follow the plant air and utilities manual, Section 6 |

citations.quote: Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. Above 66 degC the drive derates its speed, adding about 0.8 s to the cycle for every degree above that point, so the cell cycle time rises and stations downstream are starved. The 72 degC alarm comes before the 80 degC trip. A failing cabinet fan is often audible before the trip.
On ST30, check coolant flow first: a servo temperature rise that follows a fall in coolant flow is a cooling-circuit problem (see Section 6.4), not a drive problem.
A servo temperature rise with normal coolant flow and a cabinet fan that is noisy, slow or stopped points to the cabinet cooling fan or a clogged cabinet filter.

| `servo_temp_c` above 65 degC, cycle time normal | Cabinet fan failing or filter mat clogged; high ambient temperature | Listen to the cabinet fan; inspect the filter mat; compare cabinet and ambient temperature | Clean or replace the filter mat; replace the fan (see Table 7-1) |

citations.quote: A narrow bead with normal flow and pressure points to the nozzle or the bead program; a narrow bead with low flow points to the pump supply (see Section 6.2).

Outlet pressure (`pump_pressure_bar`) starts to pulse at the pump stroke rate (0.15 Hz, one stroke about every 6.7 s) and its mean falls. Flow (`flow_rate_ccm`) drops below its normal range of 270 to 330 cc/min. Motor current falls slightly and becomes unsteady because the pump moves less material.
Pressure pulsing at the stroke rate together with falling flow means the pump is not filling on each stroke: a starved inlet or cavitation, not a blocked nozzle.
A blocked nozzle raises outlet pressure and lowers flow; a starved inlet lowers both pressure and flow.

Typical signature. Tip resistance (tip_resistance_mohm) climbs steadily over hours from about 0.15 mOhm towards the 0.185 mOhm alarm limit as the tip faces pick up coating material and oxide (which raises contact resistance) and lose their shape, while the current stepper raises weld current (weld_current_ka) to compensate.
Tip resistance that rises in a straight line over several hours, together with a stepping weld current, is the signature of electrode tip wear, not of a controller fault.

citations.quote: Tip resistance that rises in a straight line over several hours, together with a stepping weld current, is the signature of electrode tip wear, not of a controller fault.

citations.quote: Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. citations.quote: Typical signature. In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (header_pressure_bar) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (compressor_current_a) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes.
When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |

citations.quote: Regulated gun air (`air_pressure_bar`) normally sits at 5.6 bar within 5.3 to 5.9 bar. Below 5 bar the cell raises a low-air alarm; at 4.6 bar the supply-air interlock stops the cell. Gun force alarms (A-ST20-GUN-FRC, A-ST30-GUN-FRC) can appear as the air falls.

When gun air pressure falls at ST20 and ST30 together, the cause is upstream in the plant air supply; check the header pressure (see Section 6.2 of AM-CA-01 (Plant Air System and Utilities)) before working on either cell.
When gun air falls at one cell only, check that cell's filter-regulator, drop-leg ball valve and quick couplings.

| Gun air low at one cell only | Filter-regulator element clogged, regulator drifted, or local leak | Read the cell gauge; listen for leaks at the drop leg and couplings | Replace the filter element; reset the regulator; repair the leak |

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.
Check drop-leg fittings and quick couplings at the weld cells first; they account for most leaks on this header.

citations.quote: | S-ST20-SRV-OT / S-ST30-SRV-OT | servo drive over-temperature trip | Drive stopped the cell; see Section 6.3 |

Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. Above 66 degC the drive derates its speed, adding about 0.8 s to the cycle for every degree above that point, so the cell cycle time rises and stations downstream are starved. The 72 degC alarm comes before the 80 degC trip. A failing cabinet fan is often audible before the trip.
On ST30, check coolant flow first: a servo temperature rise that follows a fall in coolant flow is a cooling-circuit problem (see Section 6.4), not a drive problem.

| Trip S-ST20-SRV-OT or S-ST30-SRV-OT at 80 degC | Sustained overheating not corrected at the alarm stage | Check coolant flow (ST30), the cabinet fan and the gun mechanics for binding | Let the drive cool; restart only after the cause is found |

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes.
When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

citations.quote: Each product model has its own main pressure setpoint: model A 180 bar and model B 190 bar (see Table 3-3). If the recipe for the wrong model, or a wrong value, is loaded at a changeover, main pressure (`hyd_pressure_bar`) settles at the wrong level as a clean step right after the changeover and stays there. Parts are under-formed, and the ST20 weld cell downstream starts to show weld quality alarms and scatter in tip resistance.
A step change in main pressure that starts exactly at a changeover, with oil temperature and vibration unchanged, is a recipe or setpoint error, not hydraulic wear.

Hydraulic wear develops over hours to days, not at a changeover. Four failure modes are common: internal pump leakage, a sluggish (lagging) switching valve, loss of accumulator precharge, and loss of cooler efficiency. Each moves pressure, motor current, oil temperature, vibration and cycle time in its own pattern; use Table 6-3 to tell them apart.
Pressure sagging below setpoint while motor current rises and oil temperature creeps up indicates internal pump leakage.

citations.quote: A real process change moves more than one signal; a single tag that trends steadily while every physically related tag stays normal points to the instrument, not the process.

Gaps in a trend, a value that stays exactly constant for a long period (stuck value) and the same alarm repeating several times within a minute (alarm chatter) are data-quality effects of the instrument or the network; they are not process faults and are not evidence of a failure.

| One tag trends steadily towards a limit; all related tags in Table 6-5 stay normal | Transmitter drift (ageing, contamination, loose terminal, moisture in the connector) | Compare the reading with a calibrated handheld reference at the same point; inspect the connector and cable | Recalibrate or replace the transmitter; record the as-found and as-left values in the calibration log |

| Same alarm raised and cleared several times within a minute | Alarm chatter: value hovering at the limit with too little deadband | Check the trend at the limit; check the alarm deadband setting | Treat as one event; request a deadband review through change control (see Chapter 5) |

citations.quote: A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.
When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |

| Header pressure low, compressor current low (not loading) | Inlet valve stuck closed, or load control fault | Check the compressor display for load status and faults | Repair the inlet valve or load control |

citations.quote: Drive-end bearing vibration (`vibration_rms_mms`) rises out of its normal range of 0.8 to 2.8 mm/s, slowly at first and then faster. The one-second RMS trend carries a ripple at the pulley rotation frequency (about 0.255 Hz at 12 m/min, one turn every 3.9 s). Bearing temperature (`bearing_temp_c`) follows some minutes later; motor current rises slightly and chain speed sags.
Vibration that grows in an accelerating curve, with a ripple at the pulley rotation frequency and a delayed rise in bearing temperature, indicates a drive-end bearing defect.
In the high-rate vibration spectrum, a bearing defect shows peaks at the bearing defect frequencies and their harmonics; calculate them from the bearing geometry on the bearing data sheet.
